article.description: A complete guide to understanding JDK, JRE, and JVM in Java — their differences, internal architecture, components (class loader, JIT, GC), memory model, and how bytecode executes end-to-end.
article.keywords: jdk vs jre vs jvm, jvm architecture, class loader, jit compiler, garbage collector, java heap, java stack, bytecode, java memory model, jvm internals

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?

acceptedAnswer.text: JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the engine that executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence. JRE (Java Runtime Environment) = JVM + Java Class Libraries — the minimum needed to RUN a Java application. JDK (Java Development Kit) = JRE + Developer Tools (javac compiler, javadoc, jdb debugger, jar) — needed to WRITE, COMPILE, and RUN Java programs. Think of it as: JDK contains JRE, which contains JVM.

JVM architecture has three main subsystems: (1) Class Loader Subsystem — loads, links, and initializes .class files. (2) Runtime Data Areas — memory regions including Heap (objects), Stack (method frames), Method Area (class metadata), PC Register, and Native Method Stack. (3) Execution Engine — contains the Interpreter (executes bytecode line by line), JIT Compiler (compiles hot bytecode to native code), and Garbage Collector (automatic memory management).

mainEntity.name: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: JIT (Just-In-Time) Compiler is a component of the JVM Execution Engine that improves Java performance. Initially, the JVM interprets bytecode line by line (slow). The JIT compiler monitors execution and identifies frequently executed code sections called 'hot spots'. It then compiles these hot spots directly into native machine code. Subsequent executions use the native code, making Java programs run significantly faster — approaching the speed of C++ in long-running applications.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Heap and Stack memory in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Stack memory is per-thread, LIFO-structured, and stores method call frames — local variables and method call information. It is fast, automatically managed, and has limited size. Heap memory is shared across all threads and stores all objects and instance variables created with 'new'. It is larger, managed by the Garbage Collector, and can cause OutOfMemoryError if full. Primitive local variables go to Stack; Objects always go to Heap.

mainEntity.name: What is the Garbage Collector in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Java Garbage Collector (GC) is an automatic memory management system built into the JVM. It identifies objects on the Heap that are no longer reachable (no live references) and reclaims their memory. This eliminates manual memory management (no malloc/free like C++) and prevents memory leaks. Java 21 includes multiple GC algorithms: G1GC (default), ZGC (ultra-low latency), and Shenandoah — each optimized for different workloads.

articleHeader.title: JDK vs JRE vs JVM — Complete Explanation
articleHeader.subtitle: A deep-dive guide to understanding Java Development Kit, Java Runtime Environment, and Java Virtual Machine — covering JVM architecture, class loader, JIT compiler, garbage collector, heap & stack memory, and bytecode execution flow.

blocks.text: One of the most frequently asked questions in every Java interview — and one of the most confused topics for beginners — is: "What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?" These three terms are at the heart of how Java works, and understanding them clearly will give you a solid foundation for everything else in Java.

In simple terms: JVM is the engine that runs your Java program. JRE is the environment that provides JVM + standard libraries to run it. JDK is the complete toolkit that includes JRE + developer tools to write, compile, and run Java programs. The relationship is: JDK ⊇ JRE ⊇ JVM.

rows: Executes Java bytecode on any platform
Provides the environment to RUN Java apps (JVM + Libraries)
Provides tools to WRITE, COMPILE, and RUN Java apps (JRE + Dev Tools)

sections.title: What is JVM — Java Virtual Machine?

blocks.text: The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is an abstract computing machine — a software layer that acts as a virtual computer inside your real computer. It is the core reason Java is platform-independent. The JVM does not care whether the underlying hardware is Windows, Linux, or macOS — it provides a uniform execution environment for Java bytecode.
The JVM performs four primary responsibilities every time a Java program runs:

items.title: Load Code
items.text: The Class Loader reads .class bytecode files from disk, network, or memory and loads them into the JVM's Runtime Data Areas.

items.title: Verify Code
items.text: The Bytecode Verifier checks every loaded .class file for structural validity, type safety, and security violations — before a single instruction executes.

items.title: Execute Code
items.text: The Execution Engine (Interpreter + JIT Compiler) translates bytecode instructions into native machine code and runs them on the host CPU.

items.title: Manage Memory
items.text: The Garbage Collector automatically allocates memory for new objects on the Heap and reclaims memory from objects that are no longer reachable.

blocks.text: Important: The JVM itself is platform-specific — there is a different JVM implementation for Windows, Linux, and macOS. But the bytecode it executes is platform-neutral. This is the magic of WORA — the bytecode is universal, only the JVM varies.

The JVM is not a single monolithic program — it is a carefully designed system of three interconnected subsystems. Understanding this architecture is crucial for writing performant Java code and for cracking advanced Java interviews.

sections.title: Class Loader Subsystem — How Java Loads Classes

blocks.text: The Class Loader Subsystem is the first stage of JVM execution. When your Java program starts, the JVM does not load all classes at once — it uses lazy loading, loading classes only when they are first needed. The Class Loader performs three phases:

blocks.text: Delegation Model: When a class needs to be loaded, the Application ClassLoader first delegates to the Extension ClassLoader, which delegates to the Bootstrap ClassLoader. Only if the parent cannot find the class does the child attempt to load it. This prevents malicious code from replacing core Java classes like java.lang.String.

sections.title: Runtime Data Areas — JVM Memory Model

blocks.text: The JVM divides memory into five distinct Runtime Data Areas. Understanding which data lives where is essential for writing memory-efficient Java programs and diagnosing OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError issues.

items.title: Method Area (Metaspace)
items.text: Shared across all threads. Stores class-level data: class name, parent class, method bytecode, static variables, constant pool. In Java 8+, this is called Metaspace and is in native memory (not JVM heap). StackOverflow in Metaspace is possible if too many classes are loaded dynamically.

items.title: Heap Area
items.text: Shared across all threads. This is where ALL objects and arrays are allocated (created with 'new'). Divided into Young Generation (Eden + Survivor spaces) and Old Generation. Managed by the Garbage Collector. OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space occurs when Heap is full.

items.title: Stack Area (JVM Stack)
items.text: One Stack per thread. Stores method call frames — each frame contains: local variables, operand stack, and reference to constant pool. LIFO structure — frames are pushed on method call and popped on method return. StackOverflowError occurs with infinite recursion.

items.title: PC Register (Program Counter)
items.text: One PC Register per thread. Stores the address of the currently executing bytecode instruction. When a thread switches between methods, the PC Register saves the return address so execution can resume correctly.

items.title: Native Method Stack
items.text: One per thread. Used when Java code calls native methods (C/C++ code via JNI). Similar to JVM Stack but for native code execution. Used internally by java.io for file I/O and java.net for networking.

sections.title: Execution Engine — Interpreter vs JIT Compiler

blocks.text: The Execution Engine is the heart of the JVM — it is responsible for actually running your Java bytecode. It has two strategies for executing bytecode, and understanding both explains why Java's performance has improved dramatically over the years.

rows: Reads and executes bytecode one instruction at a time
Compiles frequently-used bytecode to native machine code
Slower startup but faster sustained execution
Next-gen JIT written in Java itself (Java 21+)

blocks.text: How JIT Works: The JVM starts by interpreting all bytecode. It counts how many times each method is called. When a method crosses the invocation threshold (default: 10,000 times), the JIT compiler compiles it to native machine code. Future calls execute the native code directly — bypassing the interpreter entirely. This is why Java applications get faster over time the longer they run.

blocks.text: Java's Garbage Collector (GC) is one of its most celebrated features. Unlike C and C++ where developers manually allocate and free memory (malloc/free), Java's GC automatically identifies and reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any live thread. This prevents the two most common memory bugs: memory leaks (forgetting to free) and dangling pointers (freeing and then using).
How Garbage Collection Works — Mark & Sweep

items.text: The GC starts from GC Roots (active thread stacks, static variables, JNI references) and marks every reachable object in the Heap by traversing all references.
All objects NOT marked as reachable are considered garbage. The GC reclaims their memory.
Some GC algorithms compact live objects together to eliminate fragmentation, making future allocations faster.

sections.title: What is JRE — Java Runtime Environment?

blocks.text: The Java Runtime Environment (JRE) is the minimum software package required to run a pre-compiled Java application. It is a superset of the JVM — meaning it contains the JVM plus the standard Java class libraries that Java programs depend on.

rows: The Java Virtual Machine — executes bytecode
Core language classes: Object, String, Math, System, Thread, Exception
Extended APIs: crypto, XML, net, naming
Pre-compiled bytecode of all standard library classes

blocks.text: Who needs JRE? End users who want to run a Java application (like a JAR file) but do not intend to develop Java programs. However, since Java 9 the standalone JRE is no longer distributed — you install the JDK instead, or create a custom minimal runtime using jlink.

sections.title: What is JDK — Java Development Kit?

blocks.text: The Java Development Kit (JDK) is the complete toolkit for Java development. It is a superset of the JRE — it contains everything in the JRE plus a set of command-line developer tools. If you are a Java developer, you always install the JDK. As of Java 9, Oracle no longer ships a separate JRE — only the JDK.
The JDK is available from multiple vendors, all based on the same OpenJDK source code:

sections.title: JDK vs JRE vs JVM — Interview Questions

blocks.text: These are the most commonly asked interview questions on JDK, JRE, JVM, and Java memory model — from fresher to mid-level positions.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
items.a: JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the execution engine that runs Java bytecode and provides platform independence. JRE (Java Runtime Environment) = JVM + Java Class Libraries — the minimum needed to run a compiled Java application. JDK (Java Development Kit) = JRE + Developer Tools (javac, javap, jdb, javadoc, jar) — required to write, compile, debug, and run Java programs. The nesting relationship is: JDK ⊇ JRE ⊇ JVM.

items.q: Q2. What is JVM architecture? Name its main subsystems.
items.a: JVM architecture has three main subsystems: (1) Class Loader Subsystem — loads, links (verifies, prepares, resolves), and initializes .class files. (2) Runtime Data Areas — JVM memory: Method Area (class metadata), Heap (objects), JVM Stack (method frames), PC Register (current instruction), Native Method Stack. (3) Execution Engine — Interpreter (line-by-line execution), JIT Compiler (hot code to native), Garbage Collector (memory reclamation). Plus Native Method Interface (JNI) to call native C/C++ code.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between Heap and Stack memory in Java?
items.a: Stack is thread-private, LIFO-structured, stores method frames and local variables. It is fast, small (~256KB-1MB), auto-managed. Overflow → StackOverflowError. Heap is shared across threads, stores all objects created with 'new', managed by GC, larger (~256MB-4GB). Overflow → OutOfMemoryError. Key rule: local primitives → Stack; objects and arrays → Heap; object references → Stack (the reference) pointing to Heap (the object).

items.q: Q4. What is the JIT Compiler and how does it improve Java performance?
items.a: JIT (Just-In-Time) Compiler is part of the JVM Execution Engine. Initially, all bytecode is interpreted line-by-line (slow). The JIT monitors execution and identifies 'hot' code — methods called more than ~10,000 times. It compiles these hot methods directly to native machine code. Future calls bypass the interpreter and execute the native code directly. This is why Java apps get faster over time — the longer they run, the more code gets JIT-compiled to near-native speed.

items.q: Q5. What are the three phases of the Class Loader?
items.a: Loading: reads the .class binary and creates a Class object in Method Area. Linking: has three sub-phases — Verification (bytecode structure and type safety), Preparation (static variables allocated with default values: int→0, boolean→false, Object→null), Resolution (symbolic references like class names replaced with direct memory addresses). Initialization: static initializer blocks and static variable assignments execute top-to-bottom. This is when your static { } blocks run.

items.q: Q6. Is JVM platform-independent? Then how is Java platform-independent?
items.a: This is a classic trick question. The JVM itself is NOT platform-independent — there is a different JVM implementation for Windows (jvm.dll), Linux (libjvm.so), and macOS (libjvm.dylib). What is platform-independent is Java BYTECODE (.class files). The bytecode specification is the same everywhere. Each OS has its own JVM that knows how to execute that universal bytecode for that specific OS. So Java achieves platform independence not because JVM is universal, but because BYTECODE is universal and each JVM translates it to local native code.

items.q: Q7. What is Garbage Collection? What GC algorithms does Java 21 have?
items.a: Garbage Collection (GC) is automatic memory management — the JVM identifies objects in the Heap with no live references and reclaims their memory. Process: Mark (find all reachable objects from GC roots) → Sweep (reclaim unreachable objects) → Compact (optional, defragment). Java 21 GC algorithms: G1GC (default — balanced latency/throughput), ZGC (ultra-low latency, sub-millisecond pauses, Java 21 is production-ready), Shenandoah (low-latency, large heaps), Serial GC (single-threaded, embedded), Parallel GC (throughput-focused), Epsilon GC (no GC — for testing).

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between the java and javac commands?
items.a: javac is the Java Compiler (part of JDK only, not JRE). It takes .java source files as input and produces .class bytecode files: javac HelloWorld.java → HelloWorld.class. java is the Java Launcher (part of JRE and JDK). It starts the JVM and runs a compiled class: java HelloWorld runs the main() method in HelloWorld.class. You need JDK for javac; you only need JRE for java. Since Java 11, you can use java HelloWorld.java to compile-and-run in one step (source-code launcher).

items.q: Q9. What causes StackOverflowError and OutOfMemoryError?
items.a: StackOverflowError: occurs when the JVM Stack runs out of space. Most common cause: infinite recursion — a method calls itself endlessly, creating infinite stack frames. Each frame is ~few KB; the stack is only ~256KB-1MB. OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space: occurs when the Heap is full and GC cannot free enough memory. Usually caused by: creating objects faster than GC can collect them, memory leaks (objects referenced but unused), or loading extremely large data sets. Fix: increase heap (-Xmx4g) or fix the leak.

items.q: Q10. What happens when you run 'java HelloWorld' on the command line?
items.a: Step-by-step: (1) OS launches the JVM process. (2) JVM initializes Runtime Data Areas (Heap, Method Area, etc.). (3) Bootstrap ClassLoader loads core Java classes (java.lang.Object, etc.). (4) Application ClassLoader loads HelloWorld.class from the classpath. (5) Bytecode Verifier checks HelloWorld.class for validity. (6) JVM looks for public static void main(String[] args) in HelloWorld. (7) Execution Engine starts interpreting the main() bytecode. (8) JIT compiles hot sections. (9) System.out.println() executes — output appears. (10) main() returns, JVM initiates shutdown, GC runs final cleanup.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of JDK, JRE, and JVM concepts. Try answering each question before revealing the answer.

items.q: 1. A user wants to run a pre-compiled Java .jar application but does not want to develop Java programs. What is the minimum they need to install?
items.a: Technically JRE (Java Runtime Environment) — it contains JVM + Class Libraries, which is all that is needed to run a compiled Java application. However, since Java 9, Oracle no longer ships a standalone JRE. In practice, users install the full JDK 21, which includes the JRE. Alternatively, developers can create a minimal custom runtime using jlink that includes only the modules the application needs.

items.q: 2. Why does the JVM return 'null' when you call String.class.getClassLoader()?
items.a: Because String is loaded by the Bootstrap ClassLoader, which is implemented in native C++ code (not Java). In Java, when a ClassLoader is implemented natively, it is represented as null in the Java API. So String.class.getClassLoader() returning null is correct behavior — it means the Bootstrap ClassLoader loaded it, not the Application or Platform ClassLoader.

items.q: 3. What is the difference between Minor GC and Major GC?
items.a: Minor GC (Young Generation GC): runs when Eden space fills up. It is fast (milliseconds) because it only scans the small Young Generation. Objects that survive are moved to Survivor spaces. Major GC (Old Generation / Full GC): runs when Old Generation fills up. Slower (seconds) because it scans the entire Heap. Can cause 'stop-the-world' pauses where all application threads halt. Frequent Major GCs indicate a memory leak or undersized heap.

items.q: 4. Java is called 'interpreted' by some and 'compiled' by others. Who is right?
items.a: Both are partially right — Java is a hybrid. It is first compiled (javac compiles .java to .class bytecode — this is compilation). Then the JVM interprets bytecode initially. The JIT compiler then further compiles hot bytecode to native machine code at runtime. So Java involves: ahead-of-time compilation (javac), interpretation (JVM Interpreter), and just-in-time compilation (JIT). This makes it neither purely interpreted (like Python) nor purely compiled (like C++).

items.q: 5. If you create 100 threads in a Java application, how many JVM Stacks are there?
items.a: 100 JVM Stacks — one per thread. Each thread gets its own private JVM Stack (and its own PC Register and Native Method Stack). The Heap and Method Area (Metaspace) are shared across all 100 threads. This is why multi-threaded Java applications can have issues with Heap data (race conditions, synchronization needed) but not with Stack data (each thread's local variables are completely private).

items.q: 6. What is the String Pool and which JVM memory area does it belong to?
items.a: The String Pool (also called String Intern Pool) is a special cache in the Heap that stores unique String literals. When you write String s = "Java", the JVM checks the pool — if "Java" already exists, it returns the same reference. New String instances with identical content share the same pool entry, saving memory. Since Java 7, the String Pool is in the main Heap (was in PermGen/Method Area before Java 7). String s1 = "Java" and String s2 = "Java" point to the SAME pool object. String s3 = new String("Java") creates a new Heap object outside the pool.

items.q: 7. What is 'stop-the-world' in Java GC? Why is it a problem?
items.a: A 'stop-the-world' (STW) pause is when the JVM pauses ALL application threads to perform GC work. During this pause, no user requests are processed, no code executes — the application appears frozen. STW pauses are a problem for latency-sensitive applications: a 500ms GC pause in a financial trading system or web server can cause transaction failures or timeout errors. Modern GC algorithms (ZGC, Shenandoah) minimize STW pauses to under 1ms by doing most GC work concurrently with the application threads.

items.q: 8. What does the -Xmx and -Xms JVM flag do? Give a practical example.
items.a: -Xms sets the INITIAL heap size (allocated at JVM startup). -Xmx sets the MAXIMUM heap size (JVM will never exceed this). Example: java -Xms256m -Xmx2g MyApp — starts with 256MB heap, can grow up to 2GB. Best practice: set -Xms equal to -Xmx for server applications to avoid dynamic heap resizing overhead (java -Xms2g -Xmx2g MyApp). Too small -Xmx → OutOfMemoryError. Too large -Xmx → wastes RAM and GC takes longer. Choose based on profiling your application's actual memory usage.

sections.title: Conclusion — JDK vs JRE vs JVM Summary

blocks.text: You now have a thorough understanding of the three pillars of the Java platform. Let us consolidate everything with a final cheat-sheet summary:

rows: Execution engine — loads, verifies, and runs bytecode. Platform-specific but executes platform-neutral bytecode.
JVM + Class Libraries. Minimum needed to RUN a Java app. No compiler included.
JRE + Dev Tools (javac, jdb, javadoc, jar...). Required to DEVELOP Java apps. Always install JDK.
3 phases: Loading → Linking (Verify+Prepare+Resolve) → Initialization. 3 loaders: Bootstrap, Platform, App.
Method Area (class metadata), Heap (objects), Stack (method frames), PC Register, Native Method Stack.
Compiles frequently-executed bytecode to native machine code. Java gets faster the longer it runs.
Automatic memory management. Mark → Sweep → Compact. Default: G1GC. Ultra-low latency: ZGC.
Stack: thread-private, LIFO, local vars → StackOverflowError. Heap: shared, objects → OutOfMemoryError.
Platform-neutral intermediate format. Compiled once by javac, runs everywhere via any JVM.
JVM is platform-specific; bytecode is platform-neutral. JVM bridges the gap on every OS.

items.q: What is JVM architecture?
items.a: JVM architecture has three main subsystems: (1) Class Loader Subsystem — loads, links (verify, prepare, resolve), and initializes .class files. It also has the Native Method Interface (JNI) for calling native C/C++ code.

items.q: What is the Just-In-Time (JIT) Compiler in Java?
items.a: The JIT Compiler is part of the JVM Execution Engine. It monitors bytecode execution and identifies frequently called methods ('hot spots'). When a method is called more than ~10,000 times, JIT compiles it to native machine code. Future calls execute the native code directly — making Java applications significantly faster over time compared to pure interpretation.

items.q: What is the difference between Heap and Stack memory in Java?
items.a: Stack is thread-private, LIFO-structured, stores local variables and method frames. It is fast, small, and automatically cleared when methods return. Full Stack → StackOverflowError. Heap is shared across all threads and stores all objects created with 'new'. Managed by the Garbage Collector. Full Heap → OutOfMemoryError. Primitive local variables go to Stack; objects always go to Heap.

items.q: What is the Garbage Collector in Java?
items.a: The Java Garbage Collector (GC) automatically manages Heap memory — it identifies objects with no live references and reclaims their memory. Process: Mark (find reachable objects) → Sweep (reclaim unreachable objects) → Compact (optional defragmentation). Java 21 includes G1GC (default), ZGC (sub-millisecond pauses), Shenandoah, Parallel, and Serial GC. GC eliminates manual memory management and prevents memory leaks.
